To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the profile of liver disease in a district general Hospital is similar to that of other district hospitals in the country.

(i) the profile of liver disease in our hospital was dominated by alcoholic liver disease and that the OPCS data were unreliable; (ii) 11 patients with end stage disease were not referred for transplant assessment, and of these five died during the period of the study; (iii) the number of patients who died from liver failure was underestimated by the OPCS data, but the overall number of liver related deaths was not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the profile of liver disease in a district general hospitals and the referral patterns for patients who might benefit from liver transplants.
the profile of liver disease patients admitted to a district general hospital and the referral of patients for liver transplantation.

the following issues: (1) The accuracy of data provided by the OPCS; (2) the profile of patients admitted to the district hospital with liver disease; (3) whether the patients admitted are referred for consideration of transplantation; (4) whether patients referred for consideration of transplant receive a transplant.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a large number of patients with end-stage liver disease are not referred for consideration of transplantation and are therefore not given a chance to be cured by this potentially life-saving operation.
there are many patients who are suitable for liver transplantation but are not referred, and many who are referred and die.

the profile of liver disease in a district general is different from that reported in a national survey, that the majority of patients with liver failure are not referred for transplant assessment, and that the majority of those referred do not have a transplant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of patients admitted with end stage liver failure were not referred for consideration of transplantation, and that this is a national problem.
we are missing a large proportion of patients with liver disease who could benefit from liver transplantation.
there is an urgent need for better information on patients with liver disease, and for more efficient referral systems for patients with end stage disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there was a significant discrepancy between OPCS and case note data for patients with alcoholic liver disease.
patients with end stage alcoholic liver disease are under referred for consideration of transplant.
the majority of patients with advanced liver disease are not being referred for liver transplantation.
